data.content_ref: inline:The target's distinguishing evidence requires a panel to flag a checklist item as 'false' that is 'typically true in successful cases,' thereby catching a rare outlier. But this criterion cannot, within a single evaluation, separate a genuine reliability gain from mere compliance that happens to track the right answer. A panel could mark the item false simply because the item fails to match the surface features of the present case (compliance with the literal checklist logic), and this rejection could coincide with the correct outcome on the rare outlier by luck—exactly the confound the problem asks the proponent to rule out. Conversely, a genuine reliability gain might manifest as better-calibrated aggregate confidence or lower variance across repeated edge-case judgments rather than as a specific 'false flag' on an item that is normally true. By privileging one idiosyncratic behavioral signature (item-level false-flagging on typically-true items), the target both under-specifies alternative reliability signals and fails to show why that signature, within a single evaluation, is diagnostic of reliability rather than of mechanically-followed checklist rules that happen to land correctly on the outlier.
